questions.stem: Which statement gives the correct meaning of oxidation in terms of oxygen?

options.text: A reaction in which a substance gains oxygen
options.explanation: Gaining oxygen is the definition of oxidation, as in iron rusting or zinc taking oxygen from copper(II) oxide.

options.text: A reaction in which a substance loses oxygen
options.explanation: Losing oxygen is reduction, the exact opposite of the change described here.
options.misconception: oxidation and reduction reversed

options.text: Any reaction that produces a metal oxide as a product
options.explanation: The product alone does not decide the label; oxidation is judged by whether a substance gains oxygen during the reaction.
options.misconception: product identity mistaken for the definition

options.text: Any reaction that needs to be heated before it starts
options.explanation: Heating is a common way of supplying activation energy and says nothing about whether oxygen is gained or lost.
options.misconception: reaction conditions confused with the redox definition

questions.stem: In the reaction zinc + copper(II) oxide, which substance is reduced?

options.text: Copper(II) oxide, because it loses its oxygen
options.explanation: The oxide hands its oxygen over to zinc, and losing oxygen is reduction by definition.

options.text: Zinc, because it becomes zinc oxide
options.explanation: Zinc oxide forms because zinc has gained oxygen, and gaining oxygen is oxidation, not reduction.
options.misconception: product naming used instead of oxygen transfer

options.text: Copper, because it ends up as the free metal
options.explanation: Copper is the product of the reduction, but the substance being reduced is the copper(II) oxide that supplied the oxygen.
options.misconception: product of the change mistaken for the species changing

options.text: Neither substance, because oxygen is only moved around
options.explanation: Moving oxygen from one substance to another is exactly what makes one substance reduced and the other oxidised.
options.misconception: oxygen transfer not recognised as redox

questions.stem: Which species is the oxidising agent in Zn + CuO, ZnO + Cu?

options.text: CuO, because it supplies the oxygen
options.explanation: The oxidising agent gives oxygen to the other substance and is itself reduced in the process.

options.text: Zn, because it starts the reaction
options.explanation: Zinc takes the oxygen, which makes it the reducing agent rather than the oxidising agent.
options.misconception: agent roles swapped

options.text: ZnO, because it contains oxygen afterwards
options.explanation: The product zinc oxide is evidence that zinc was oxidised; it plays no agent role in the reaction.
options.misconception: product mistaken for an agent

options.text: Cu, because it is displaced as a metal
options.explanation: Copper is simply released when the oxide is reduced; it neither gives nor takes the oxygen.
options.misconception: displaced product mistaken for the agent

questions.stem: Why are oxidation and reduction described as redox when they occur together?

options.text: One substance gains oxygen at the same moment another loses it, so the two changes are inseparable
options.explanation: Oxidation cannot occur without reduction happening simultaneously, which is why the combined change carries one name.

options.text: Both changes need the same amount of heat to proceed
options.explanation: Sharing conditions does not link the two changes; it is the simultaneous oxygen transfer that couples them.
options.misconception: shared conditions mistaken for the coupling

options.text: They are two names for exactly the same change
options.explanation: The changes are opposite in direction; they happen together but each substance undergoes a different half.
options.misconception: opposites treated as synonyms

options.text: Redox only applies when oxygen is completely removed
options.explanation: Any simultaneous gain and loss of oxygen counts as redox; nothing needs to be fully removed.
options.misconception: all-or-nothing reading of the definition

questions.stem: Which role does zinc play in the reaction with copper(II) oxide?

options.text: It is the reducing agent because it removes the oxygen
options.explanation: Taking the oxygen away from the oxide reduces it, so zinc is named the reducing agent.

options.text: It is the oxidising agent because it becomes zinc oxide
options.explanation: Forming zinc oxide shows zinc gaining oxygen, which is oxidation of zinc, not an oxidising role.
options.misconception: own oxidation mistaken for an oxidising role

options.text: It is a catalyst because it speeds the change up
options.explanation: Zinc is consumed in the reaction to form zinc oxide, so it is a reactant, not a catalyst.
options.misconception: reactant mistaken for a catalyst

options.text: It has no defined role because only the oxide reacts
options.explanation: Both substances react: zinc gains oxygen and the oxide loses it, giving zinc a clear reducing role.
options.misconception: passive role assigned to a reactive metal

questions.stem: In Mg + Cu2+ giving Mg2+ + Cu, what has happened to the magnesium?

options.text: It has been oxidised because it lost electrons
options.explanation: Magnesium goes from the atom to Mg2+, which means two electrons have been lost, and electron loss is oxidation.

options.text: It has been reduced because its charge increased
options.explanation: The rising charge is the sign of electron loss; reduction would lower the charge by gaining electrons.
options.misconception: charge change read backwards

options.text: It has acted as the oxidising agent
options.explanation: The species being oxidised never acts as the oxidising agent; that role belongs to Cu2+, which is itself reduced.
options.misconception: agent role assigned to the species oxidised

options.text: It has not changed because sulfate stays the same
options.explanation: The sulfate ions are spectators; the magnesium itself has clearly changed into an ion.
options.misconception: spectator behaviour transferred to the reacting metal

options.text: Ions that appear unchanged on both sides of the equation
options.explanation: Because they take no part in the chemistry, they can be omitted from the ionic equation.

options.text: Ions that move fastest in solution
options.explanation: Speed of movement is not part of the definition; the test is whether the ion changes during the reaction.
options.misconception: physical behaviour confused with chemical participation

options.text: Ions that carry no charge at all
options.explanation: Spectator ions are fully charged, such as the sulfate ion; what defines them is that they never change.
options.misconception: uncharged particles mistaken for spectators

options.text: Ions that form the solid product of the reaction
options.explanation: In this reaction nothing solid forms; the spectators simply stay dissolved and unchanged.
options.misconception: precipitation assumed

questions.stem: Which half equation correctly shows the oxidation of magnesium?

options.text: Mg gives Mg2+ + 2e-
options.explanation: The two lost electrons appear on the product side, which is the signature of oxidation.

options.text: Mg2+ + 2e- gives Mg
options.explanation: That equation shows electrons being gained, which is the reduction of magnesium ions, not oxidation of the metal.
options.misconception: reduction half equation offered for oxidation

options.text: Mg gives Mg+ + e-
options.explanation: Magnesium forms 2+ ions here, so one electron and a 1+ ion do not match the observed change.
options.misconception: ion charge miscounted

options.text: Mg + 2e- gives Mg2+
options.explanation: Placing the electrons on the left adds negative charge while the ion's charge rises, which cannot balance.
options.misconception: electron side chosen without checking charge balance

questions.stem: What does the mnemonic OIL RIG remind you of?

options.text: Oxidation Is Loss and Reduction Is Gain, in terms of electrons
options.explanation: The mnemonic pairs each change with the electron movement that defines it.

options.text: Oxidation Is Loss and Reduction Is Gain, in terms of oxygen
options.explanation: In oxygen language the directions are reversed; OIL RIG refers only to electron transfer.
options.misconception: oxygen wording attached to the electron mnemonic

options.text: Oxidation Is Last and Reduction Is Instant
options.explanation: The mnemonic makes no claim about timing; it records which change loses and which gains electrons.
options.misconception: mnemonic letters misread

options.text: Only metals can be oxidised in any reaction
options.explanation: OIL RIG describes electron transfer for any species; ions such as Cu2+ and Fe3+ are reduced in the examples given.
options.misconception: electron transfer restricted to metals

questions.stem: In the redox reaction between Fe and Cu2+, why is Cu2+ called the oxidising agent?

options.text: Because it takes electrons from the iron and is itself reduced
options.explanation: Removing electrons oxidises the iron, and the species that does this while gaining electrons itself is the oxidising agent.

options.text: Because it donates electrons to the iron
options.explanation: Cu2+ gains electrons rather than giving them away; the donor here is the iron atom.
options.misconception: electron donor and acceptor swapped

options.text: Because copper is more reactive than iron
options.explanation: Reactivity does not decide the agent label; the species reduced while oxidising the other one is the oxidising agent.
options.misconception: reactivity order used to assign the agent

options.text: Because the sulfate ions push the copper out
options.explanation: The sulfate ions are spectators and participate in none of the electron transfer.
options.misconception: spectator ions given an active role
